claims.text: At the eastern end of the Hypostyle Hall, west of the Fourth Pylon.
Amenhotep III constructed this pylon using dismantled earlier monuments in its foundations and fill. Later incorporation into Sety I’s hall changed the appearance of its western façade.
The decoration includes Amenhotep III’s jubilee and the sacred bark on a journey to Luxor.
A planned colonnade before the pylon is a scholarly proposal; the reason for moving the entrance eastward is unknown.

sections.heading: Where you are
paragraphs: The Third Pylon closes the east end of the Great Hypostyle Hall. When Amenhotep III built it, it was the front of the temple, with open ground in front of it; Sety I later filled that space with the Hall and hid the pylon’s west face behind a stone lining.
Building it, Amenhotep III cleared away the festival court of Thutmose II with its pillars and bark shrines. The temple’s main entrance moved east, the opposite of the usual westward growth.
look: Stand at the east end of the Hall’s central aisle: the gateway in front of you is the Third Pylon’s.

sections.heading: A pylon full of older chapels
paragraphs: The monuments Amenhotep III took down did not go to waste. Their blocks were packed into the pylon’s foundations and towers as fill, and that is why many of them survived, often in fairly good condition.

When the pylon was restored in the early 20th century, several hundred blocks came out of it. From them Egyptologists rebuilt the White Chapel of Senusret I and the Red Chapel of Hatshepsut, and this material makes up most of today’s Open Air Museum. Amenhotep I’s calcite chapel came from the pylon too, and a few blocks of small alabaster shrines of Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV were found in its core.
look: The White Chapel and the Red Chapel in the Open Air Museum, north of the Great Court: both stood inside this pylon for more than three thousand years.

sections.heading: Amun’s river barge on the back of the pylon
paragraphs: On the back of the north tower, facing east, a huge scene shows the gilded barge of Amun-Ra being towed by the king’s own boat. Digital Karnak describes it as the god’s festival journey to Luxor Temple. Amenhotep III appears twice beside the temple-like cabin that held the god’s portable shrine on the river.

The scene was reworked by four later reigns. Akhenaten defaced the small scenes on the hull and Tutankhamun restored them. Horemheb erased a small figure of a king standing behind Amenhotep III, most likely Tutankhamun, and put a table of food offerings in its place, and enlarged the figures of the gods. Much later, Christian iconoclasts pecked at the faces.
look: Behind the figure of Amenhotep III, the offering table that replaced an erased king.
Faces pecked away on the figures.

sections.heading: The porch that father and son decorated
paragraphs: The gate on the west face had a porch, begun under Amenhotep III and completed by his son Amenhotep IV, the future Akhenaten. Its scenes showed the king in the traditional way, striking down enemies; the decoration was never finished.

Some scenes showed the young Amenhotep IV together with his father; they were later defaced. Sety I covered the Akhenaten scenes on the north part of the porch with stone when he built the Hall. That wall has since been taken apart and reassembled in the Open Air Museum.
look: In the Open Air Museum, the rebuilt wall of Akhenaten’s scenes from this porch.

sections.heading: Flagpoles that disappeared
paragraphs: Like the other pylons, the towers had tall wooden flagstaffs with coloured banners, standing in square notches in the front. When Sety I enclosed the west face inside the Hall, the flagstaffs were taken down.

questions.text: Did Amenhotep III plan a colonnade in front of the pylon, like the one at Luxor Temple? Scholars have suggested it; it was never built.
Did Akhenaten build a pillared court with images of Nefertiti in front of the pylon? This has been proposed, not proven.
